title: Happy 45th birthday to the IBM PC and Model F/XT
excerpt: A celebration into the IBM PC, the Model F/XT keyboard, where it came from and what it became
content_html:
• Published 12th August 2026
  • Updated 13th August 2026
  • Est. Reading Time: ~20-24 minutes

45 years ago today, on 12th August 1981, the computing landscape changed forever. IBM launched the Personal Computer (type 5150), which kickstarted a series of events that defined what most people today think a PC is, even if it was not the first computer to be called "personal". It was the vessel that kickstarted x86's popularity in computing at offices and homes alike. The PC's long-term staying power was not a feat IBM achieved alone - the IBM-compatible "clone" PC market is what helped sustain the ecosystem's prominence. Personally, I like to think a big part of the PC's initial success was its keyboard. Not the perfect layout as most may agree, but certainly a competent, well-built keyboard - the Model F/XT. Thus to celebrate, in the most appropriate way for Admiral Shark's Keyboards, we will look at this keyboard, where it came from, and what it became. Of course, with context as needed, including what led to the IBM PC, and both who and what was behind it.

Contents

Before the PC, IBM released products adjacent to a personal computer, and toyed with the idea of a personal computer throughout the 1970s. The PC's type number, 5150, places it in the lineage of the 5100 Portable Computer, and the 5110 and 5120 Computing Systems. 5100 in turn is an evolution of a prototype computer known as SCAMP (Special Computer APL Machine Portable), which was developed at the IBM Palo Alto Scientific Center in 1973.[4] William C. Lowe, an executive in the IBM General Systems Division (GSD) at the time, was considered instrumental in foresting this prototype. The 5100 was touted as a "personal computer" by some in the media, but it was a very expensive and not accessible to many people. It was notable for being portable though (for 1975), emphasised as IBM's smallest computing system to date.[5]

Tommy R. Hardy, a now-veteran IBM designer, conceptualised some interim ideas for a personal computer, including the "Yellow Bird" in 1976 and the "Aquarius" in 1977, both vaguely wedge-shaped in a form factor not unlike the later Commodore VIC-20, 64, etc., albeit bigger. Aquarius even made it to a pre-production prototype, but ultimately dismissed due to lack of confidence in its use of bubble memory modules. When Atari's 8-bit computers launched in 1979, IBM also considered aquiring Atari and utilising the 800 as a basis for the PC. Hardy conceputalised a pearl-white, IBM-branded 800 to this end,[6] but this idea proceeded no further. The next big thing, though, is Datamaster.

It would be impossible to have a discussion about the PC and its keyboard without talking about the IBM System/23 Datamaster, an influential experience for IBM that aided them in the PC's development and its keyboard. The 5322, the original "desktop" (all-in-one) Datamaster, was released in July 1981. It was followed by the 5324 "floortop" (tower) Datamaster, announced on 18th May 1982.[10] They were Intel 8085-based microcomputers intended to run business applications written in BASIC.

The development for Datamaster began in February 1978, and its hardware was ready by July 1980. However, as recalled by IBM engineer David J. Bradley, who worked on Datamaster, its launch was delayed by a year and to just a month before PC thanks to IBM deciding to develop the Datamaster's BASIC more in line with the IBM System/34 midrange computer's implementation of it.[11] The 5322's styling is attributed to Hardy via its U.S. design patent (275,285), which was filed on 4th February 1980. The design at that stage was largely like the finished product, though the keyboard layout is slightly different, with extra keys and a non-stepped Enter key. If design patents for 5324 exist, I was not able to find them during my research.

The Datamaster keyboard establishes the basis for every other keyboard discussed today. It is presently the earliest confirmed Model F keyboard implementation to make it to market, which would soon expand into an entire family of IBM flagship keyboards prominent for the first half of the '80s. They all use capacitive buckling springs, a keyswitch design by Richard Hunter Haris (U.S. utility patent 4,118,611), where pressing a key compresses a metal coil spring underneath in a way that it eventually "catastrophically" buckles, which in turn pivots a small plate made of a capacitive material atop a capacitance-sensing PCB called a "pad card". The keyboard assembly this all sits in is largely metallic, with a steel frame holding the keyswitch barrels at the top, and a usually-chromated steel base plate at the bottom.

The 5322 keyboard is a complete sub-assembly (CSA) that sits inside the host Datamaster. The keys are arranged in a layout derived from the Model B-based IBM 5251/5252 Display Station Typewriter Keyboard, which was IBM's most immediate and common pre-Datamaster major keyboard design. The aforementioned pad card bears a 12x8 key matrix and an Intel 8048 as its controller. The keyboard uses a parallel-style interface where an inverted 7-bit scancode is sent across separate scanbit lines together. Like its layout, its scancodes are also derived from the 5250 family. On the receiving end, according to RetroAND (bitspassats.com), the Datamaster has an 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface configured for mode 1 input. As the keyboard is completely internalised, it connects directly to the 5322 motherboard (CPU planar board) via an 8x2 header.

As the 5324 is a distributed system, its version of the keyboard is discrete, connecting to its host via a DB-25-terminating cable. Chronologically, this was released after the PC, so it derives its styling from the PC's keyboard, but with a considerably enlarged cover set and slightly longer riser feet. It may sometimes be confused with the IBM 5291/5292 keyboard also discussed later, but the 5324 keyboard has the larger bezel between them, to the point it sometimes gets nicknamed the "bezelmaster" Model F keyboard. The 5324 keyboard reuses the 5322's keyboard CSAs. But the 5324 keyboard adds a "keyboard adapter card" before its external cable. As explained to me by RetroAND, it has positive buffers and double negations for the control signals, likely to reduce noise. In effect, it prepares a design that was originally integrated into something, to be a distributed design that requires a longer cable.

Personal Computer

Roll back the clock to July 1980: Lowe pitched the idea of a small, low-cost business and consumer computer to IBM CEO Frank Cary, who subsequently gave him a month to develop a prototype and to launch the finished product in a year. It was dubbed "Project Chess". Lowe was promoted soon after, so Chess fell to Philip Donald (Don) Estridge. Both have been referred to as the "Father of the IBM PC".[17][18] The team consisted of about twelve engineers, who were famously able to develop the PC outside of IBM's typical processes, ultimately allowing them to meet the one-year deadline, rather than complete it in 2 to 5 years like most other IBM systems of the time.

The earliest sketches of what became the PC, from 10th August 1980, were only relatively recently published. They show that a lot of what became the PC was nailed early on, including its use of the Intel 8088, five expansion slots, two floppy diskette drives, use of ASCII instead of EBCDIC, and a detached Model F-based keyboard. There are some notable differences, of course, including the display controller, the power supply unit's location inside the PC, and that it originally specified 8" floppy diskette drives instead of 5¼".[19]

To achieve their goal, the team was also assisted by prior experience with developing Datamaster, and using readily available components. The PC's use of an Intel CPU, various Intel supporting controllers and timer, and 8-bit ISA bus were derived from Datamaster's use of similar technologies. The choice of an 8088 with 20-bit/1MB address space was largely informed by woes with Datamaster's 8085 and its 16-bit/64KB address space. The choice of 8088 over 8086 was down to savings that could be had by needing to support just an 8-bit data bus instead of 16.[11]

As you know, the IBM 5150 Personal Computer was released 45 years ago today. Its importance cannot be overstated. Its open architecture and use of the 8086-sibling Intel 8088 established one of the most popular and long-lived computer ecosystems. For better or worse nowadays, the combination of it and a Microsoft-sourced operating system is still relevant thanks to this. To me personally, learning about it and tinkering with its descendants are the backdrop to my technical interests and knowledge. The PC was joined by the IBM 5160 Personal Computer XT (PC/XT) on 8th March 1983. Over the original PC, the PC/XT adds a built-in hard drive and 3 expansion slots,[20] otherwise being a very similar design. Whilst there are many factors as to why the PC succeeded, it was certainly aided by the inclusion of a competent keyboard.

The IBM Personal Computer Keyboard is often colloquially referred to as the "XT keyboard" or "Model F/XT", using its association with the PC/XT to differentiate it from the later IBM Personal Computer AT Keyboard ("Model F/AT"). Components of the F/XT can also be referred to as being "XT". At its core, the F/XT has a keyboard assembly much like the Datamaster's, but it adopted a new serial-based protocol retroactively called IBM PC Mode 1 (also known as the "XT keyboard interface", naturally). It emits 9-bit data packets facilitating IBM scancode set 1. The keycap nomenclature was changed to ASCII style instead of EBCDIC. In the aforementioned sketches, the interface and nomenclature were decided from the beginning, but it was also supposed they may cost-save the design by eliminating the leftmost function key bank,[19] which did not come to fruition.

I was not able to find any design patents for the PC itself (if they existed), but the keyboard's (U.S. design patent 278,063) is known. Tommy Hardy is also cited for this work, as is Edward Chamberlain, Nicholas M. Leon, Peter J. Mendel (who would later work on many other keyboard-related IBM product designs), and Michael H. Sharp. Two major variants of the original F/XT are known, both with their own nuances and differences or similarities to the Datamaster keyboards. They are referred to as Type 1 and Type 2.

The original design, Type 1, is very rare today. I have only seen examples with "81" date codes on either its chips or stamped somewhere inside the cover set, so I imagine it was phased out quickly in favour of Type 2. What is interesting is that IBM chose a different approach to Datamaster for its electronics. It has a 24x4 key matrix, and the controller is split into a capacitance-sensing driver and demultiplexer on the pad card, and a separate daughterboard with an Intel 8048 as its controller. The reason for this design may be explained by the IBM 5291/5292's existence.

A telltale sign from the outside is that its original cable's 180° 5-pin DIN plug has no black plastic jacket like Type 2. The keyboard also has a reset line, which the IBM PC Technical Reference implies was not used[24] and is entirely dropped by Type 2.

The Type 2 design is what most F/XTs actually are, and certainly by the time of PC/XT, the only one available. As already mentioned, their DIN plugs have a plastic jacket and lack a reset line. But much has changed internally too, perhaps anarchonistic in some ways. It reverts to using a 12x8 matrix like Datamaster's, though configured differently. The controller is unified with the pad card once again, though of course still implementing the IBM PC Mode 1 interface.

The IBM 5291 Model 1 Display Station and 5292 Color Display Station were both 5250-family terminals announced on 6th September 1982. They are plug-compatible with the '70s IBM 5251 Display Station (model 11), [29][30] though the 5291 was intended as a low-cost replacement and the 5292 as a colour-enhanced supplement. 5291 Model 2 joined them on 2nd October 1984,[31] which was functionally identical to 5291-1 but smaller, more ergonomic, and with a relocatable screen, whereas 5291's was tightly integrated into the base unit.

The 529X keyboard is a fun one. It's like the F/XT but dialled up to eleven. It has considerable bezels just like the 5324's, though with a slightly smaller 'forehead'. But it also has absurd three-setting riser feet, the longest of an IBM keyboard I have seen. Perhaps both of these facts lend themselves to the 529X keyboard's common nickname - the "bigfoot" Model F. The key nomenclature is back to being 5250-style, given 5291's and 5292's application. The 529X keyboard CSA is the same as the Type 1 F/XT's but without the controller daughtercard. Instead, the terminal itself would be its controller, making the 529X keyboard effectively "brainless" on their own. This is where I can see why IBM designed the Type 1 F/XT differently from Datamaster - more component commonality between higher-volume products. Both PC and (in my observations) at least 5291 were more so than Datamaster. Ultimately, the simpler, more elegant Type 2 solution won out for PCs, though.

The 5291-2 and 5292 shared the same completely detachable keyboard with a DA-15 plug, dubbed the Type 2 529X keyboard. 5291-1's Type 1 was instead always tethered, as its cable connected to a 14-pin IDC-style header inside the terminal, meaning the terminal has to be opened to detach it. The Type 2 is typically the far more common of the two today.

Of all the keyboards discussed today, the 529X keyboard was produced the longest. Lexmark, which was founded from IBM Information Products Corporation's divestiture on 27th March 1991,[34] produced 529X keyboards into at least mid-1994. This also makes it one of the last Model Fs in production in general. Lexmark also refurbished existing 529X keyboards into 1996, their final year in the keyboard business. Lexmark-produced and Lexmark-refurbished 529X keyboards can usually be distinguished by the latter being mislabelled "Model M" on their rear labels instead of "F".

The IBM Instruments Computer System 9000 (CS/9000, also known simply as the System 9000) was a Motorola 68000-powered laboratory computer introduced in May 1982. It was notable for its vertical stack including an integrated printer/plotter and a 57-key membrane touch panel. On 21st February 1984, IBM introduced the System 9002 Desk-Top Computer and renamed the CS/9000 to the System 9001 Bench-Top Computer. In Q2 1985, the System 9003 Industrial-Floor Computer also joined them.[36]

The 9002 was designed to be a space-saving alternative to the now-9001, shedding the printer/plotter and integrating the membrane touch panel into the keyboard itself.[37] The 9003 was intended for use in manufacturing and process control applications, being able to operate as standalone or link with an IBM host processor via Systems Network Architecture (SNA). The entire 9000 family was withdrawn effective 2nd December 1986,[38] as ultimately all three members were unsuccessful in their respective markets.

The CS/9000 and 9001 used the IBM System 9000 Standard Keyboard, which was designed to sit on top of a protrusion from the host computer. The Standard Keyboard notably sports a rectangular "IBM System 9000" branding, no flip-out riser feet, a cable that sprouts from the left, and a choke just before the cable's DIN plug. Otherwise, it is the same and electrically compatible with the standard F/XT.

The 9002's keyboard - the IBM System 9002 Hybrid Keyboard - is a lot more interesting, though. As aforementioned, this keyboard notably integrates the 57-key membrane touch panel into the keyboard itself. Presumably, "Hybrid" refers to its nature of having both a buckling-spring keyboard and the touch panel. The resultant design is very reminiscent of the IBM 104-key Model F Converged Keyboard used for the IBM 3290 Information Panel and 5085 Graphics Processor, with the panel taking the place of the 24-function-key bank but retaining its noticable bezels and two-stage riser feet. Despite this, the keyboard itself remains the F/XT-style assembly.

Whilst a 9002 computer has turned up in recent times, the keyboard has not, nor are there any photos of the keyboard from outside the 1980s. No one that I know owns one to test it or dig inside, thus its electronics remain a mystery to me. In my 'professional' opinion, the 9002 Hybrid Keyboard is the rarest Model F keyboard known, perhaps at most tied with another keyboard I plan to talk about soon. At least all the other known variants have been contemporaneously pictured...

At present, the 9003 or its keyboard also remain unseen to me. Computerworld's reporting suggests the keyboard and 57-key touch panel were separate, just like the 9001.[41]

Portable Personal Computer

On 16th February 1984, IBM announced the 5155 Portable Personal Computer. It is essentially a PC/XT assembled into a luggable form and given a cute 9" amber CRT display and one or two now-half-height 5¼" floppy diskette drives.[43] It was IBM's answer to the Compaq Portable, one of the first IBM PC clones that launched just under a year earlier and happened to be in the same form factor.

Compared to the original F/XT, the 5155's version is housed in an all-plastic, two-tone cover set with a compartment to stuff its cable into, its base plate is a shiny, silvery aluminium instead of chromated steel, and it has a 6-pin modular plug instead of DIN. This results in the keyboard being considerably lighter and sounding somewhat higher-pitched than the original. The cover set can also be opened toolessly as the dark plastic bezel surrounding the keys can be lifted at any time. Electrically, the keyboard remains unchanged, and it can be passively adapted to 5-pin DIN if so desired.

When not in use, the keyboard should be mounted upright to the front of the 5155, covering its entire front. The keyboard has two clips towards the top that are used to release it and allow it to pivot down. You can additionally deploy its riser feet to completely detach the keyboard from the host PC.

TPC and EMR

The IBM Tempest PC (TPC) family are IBM PC-related products that were designed or modified to qualify under the TEMPEST program. TEMPEST is a NATO-recognised, United States National Security Agency specification regarding protecting against spying with electronic equipment. In particular, qualifying systems are designed not to radiate electromagnetic emanations to counter Van Eck phreaking. IBM referred to such systems as being 'TEMPESTed', usually adding special covers and filters to meet the requirements. The TPC family ultimately included the IBM 4450 TPC1 (TEMPESTed PC), 4455 TPC2 (PC/XT), 4456 TPC3 (3270 PC), 4459 TPC4 (PC/AT), and 4460 TPC5 (3270 PC/AT).[44]

TPC1 and TPC2 indeed come with an F/XT variant named TPC Keyboard I and TPC Keyboard II, respectively, which despite their name and part numbers, do not differ from each other. Additionally, an IBM EMR Keyboard and EMR Keyboard II are known, although it is presently unclear to me what exactly those two were used for (ie., are they also TPC family products or are they intended for TEMPESTed IBM systems outside of the TPC family).

All four keyboards have clay covering the controller, hardier, non-coiled cables, and unique plugs compared to their 'civilian' counterparts. EMR I uniquely used a 180° 5-pin DIN plug not unlike the Type 1 F/XT's, whereas the other three (and TPCs 3 through 5) used a DE-9 connector instead. This means EMR I is not physically compatible with the known TPCs. EMR II, however, seems to be identical to TPC1 and TPC2.

Regarding the PCs themselves, at least based on Cathode Ray Dude's analysis on the TPC4 and comparison with a standard PC/AT, they appear to be mostly as you would expect from the standard models inside. The motherboard, power supply and ISA card complement were typical, and the differences lay with the reinforced outer casing, the power switch location and function, and some buffer space between the rear I/O and the actual back of the TPC.[51]

It is worth briefly mentioning the IBM 5531 Industrial Computer and its keyboard. The IBM 5531 Industrial Computer was an industrialised version of the PC/XT, introduced on 1st May 1984. It was intended for use on factory floors and accordingly designed to be more resistant to harsher physical conditions.[55] Being PC/XT-based, it thus received an XT-style keyboard. Whilst it superficially looks like an industrial-grey version of the F/XT, the keyboard is of an unrelated design and not considered a Model F keyboard. It was made by Oak Switch Systems for IBM, using their Full-Travel Membrane (FTM) keyswitches. To easily tell it a part from the F/XT, note its flatter appearance and the lack of curvature on the separator between the F-keys and the rest of the keys. This is not to say this keyboard does not have any merit; just note that it is indeed not a Model F and you should not expect it to be like one.

The next big thing, though, is Datamaster.5324 Datamaster[9]It would be impossible to have a discussion about the PC and its keyboard without talking about the IBM System/23 Datamaster, an influential experience for IBM that aided them in the PC's development and its keyboard. The 5322, the original "desktop" (all-in-one) Datamaster, was released in July 1981. It was followed by the 5324 "floortop" (tower) Datamaster, announced on 18th May 1982.[10] They were Intel 8085-based microcomputers intended to run business applications written in BASIC.The development for Datamaster began in February 1978, and its hardware was ready by July 1980. However, as recalled by IBM engineer David J. Bradley, who worked on Datamaster, its launch was delayed by a year and to just a month before PC thanks to IBM deciding to develop the Datamaster's BASIC more in line with the IBM System/34 midrange computer's implementation of it.[11] The 5322's styling is attributed to Hardy via its U.S. design patent (275,285), which was filed on 4th February 1980. The design at that stage was largely like the finished product, though the keyboard layout is slightly different, with extra keys and a non-stepped Enter key. If design patents for 5324 exist, I was not able to find them during my research.5322 keyboard (top)[8]5322 CSA (bottom)[13]The Datamaster keyboard establishes the basis for every other keyboard discussed today. It is presently the earliest confirmed Model F keyboard implementation to make it to market, which would soon expand into an entire family of IBM flagship keyboards prominent for the first half of the '80s. They all use capacitive buckling springs, a keyswitch design by Richard Hunter Haris (U.S. utility patent 4,118,611), where pressing a key compresses a metal coil spring underneath in a way that it eventually "catastrophically" buckles, which in turn pivots a small plate made of a capacitive material atop a capacitance-sensing PCB called a "pad card". The keyboard assembly this all sits in is largely metallic, with a steel frame holding the keyswitch barrels at the top, and a usually-chromated steel base plate at the bottom.The 5322 keyboard is a complete sub-assembly (CSA) that sits inside the host Datamaster. The keys are arranged in a layout derived from the Model B-based IBM 5251/5252 Display Station Typewriter Keyboard, which was IBM's most immediate and common pre-Datamaster major keyboard design. The aforementioned pad card bears a 12x8 key matrix and an Intel 8048 as its controller. The keyboard uses a parallel-style interface where an inverted 7-bit scancode is sent across separate scanbit lines together. Like its layout, its scancodes are also derived from the 5250 family. On the receiving end, according to RetroAND (bitspassats.com), the Datamaster has an 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface configured for mode 1 input. As the keyboard is completely internalised, it connects directly to the 5322 motherboard (CPU planar board) via an 8x2 header.5324 keyboard (top)[14]5324 keyboard (bottom)[14]5324 daughterboard (top)[15]5324 daughterboard (bottom)[15]As the 5324 is a distributed system, its version of the keyboard is discrete, connecting to its host via a DB-25-terminating cable. Chronologically, this was released after the PC, so it derives its styling from the PC's keyboard, but with a considerably enlarged cover set and slightly longer riser feet. It may sometimes be confused with the IBM 5291/5292 keyboard also discussed later, but the 5324 keyboard has the larger bezel between them, to the point it sometimes gets nicknamed the "bezelmaster" Model F keyboard. The 5324 keyboard reuses the 5322's keyboard CSAs. But the 5324 keyboard adds a "keyboard adapter card" before its external cable. As explained to me by RetroAND, it has positive buffers and double negations for the control signals, likely to reduce noise. In effect, it prepares a design that was originally integrated into something, to be a distributed design that requires a longer cable.Personal ComputerAn IBM Personal Computer (base unit)[16]Roll back the clock to July 1980: Lowe pitched the idea of a small, low-cost business and consumer computer to IBM CEO Frank Cary, who subsequently gave him a month to develop a prototype and to launch the finished product in a year. It was dubbed "Project Chess". Lowe was promoted soon after, so Chess fell to Philip Donald (Don) Estridge. Both have been referred to as the "Father of the IBM PC".[17][18] The team consisted of about twelve engineers, who were famously able to develop the PC outside of IBM's typical processes, ultimately allowing them to meet the one-year deadline, rather than complete it in 2 to 5 years like most other IBM systems of the time.The earliest sketches of what became the PC, from 10th August 1980, were only relatively recently published. They show that a lot of what became the PC was nailed early on, including its use of the Intel 8088, five expansion slots, two floppy diskette drives, use of ASCII instead of EBCDIC, and a detached Model F-based keyboard. There are some notable differences, of course, including the display controller, the power supply unit's location inside the PC, and that it originally specified 8" floppy diskette drives instead of 5¼".[19]To achieve their goal, the team was also assisted by prior experience with developing Datamaster, and using readily available components. The PC's use of an Intel CPU, various Intel supporting controllers and timer, and 8-bit ISA bus were derived from Datamaster's use of similar technologies. The choice of an 8088 with 20-bit/1MB address space was largely informed by woes with Datamaster's 8085 and its 16-bit/64KB address space. The choice of 8088 over 8086 was down to savings that could be had by needing to support just an 8-bit data bus instead of 16.[11]An IBM Personal Computer[16]As you know, the IBM 5150 Personal Computer was released 45 years ago today. Its importance cannot be overstated. Its open architecture and use of the 8086-sibling Intel 8088 established one of the most popular and long-lived computer ecosystems. For better or worse nowadays, the combination of it and a Microsoft-sourced operating system is still relevant thanks to this. To me personally, learning about it and tinkering with its descendants are the backdrop to my technical interests and knowledge. The PC was joined by the IBM 5160 Personal Computer XT (PC/XT) on 8th March 1983. Over the original PC, the PC/XT adds a built-in hard drive and 3 expansion slots,[20] otherwise being a very similar design. Whilst there are many factors as to why the PC succeeded, it was certainly aided by the inclusion of a competent keyboard.The IBM Personal Computer Keyboard[21]Type 1 vs 2 F/XT (top)[22]Type 1 vs 2 F/XT (CSA bottom)[22]The IBM Personal Computer Keyboard is often colloquially referred to as the "XT keyboard" or "Model F/XT", using its association with the PC/XT to differentiate it from the later IBM Personal Computer AT Keyboard ("Model F/AT"). Components of the F/XT can also be referred to as being "XT". At its core, the F/XT has a keyboard assembly much like the Datamaster's, but it adopted a new serial-based protocol retroactively called IBM PC Mode 1 (also known as the "XT keyboard interface", naturally). It emits 9-bit data packets facilitating IBM scancode set 1. The keycap nomenclature was changed to ASCII style instead of EBCDIC. In the aforementioned sketches, the interface and nomenclature were decided from the beginning, but it was also supposed they may cost-save the design by eliminating the leftmost function key bank,[19] which did not come to fruition.I was not able to find any design patents for the PC itself (if they existed), but the keyboard's (U.S. design patent 278,063) is known. Tommy Hardy is also cited for this work, as is Edward Chamberlain, Nicholas M. Leon, Peter J. Mendel (who would later work on many other keyboard-related IBM product designs), and Michael H. Sharp. Two major variants of the original F/XT are known, both with their own nuances and differences or similarities to the Datamaster keyboards. They are referred to as Type 1 and Type 2.Type 1 F/XT (top)[22]Type 1 F/XT CSA (bottom)[22]Type 1 F/XT CSA (open)[23]Type 1 F/XT pad card[22]Type 1 F/XT controller daughtercard[22]Type 1 F/XT possible data stamp[22]The original design, Type 1, is very rare today. I have only seen examples with "81" date codes on either its chips or stamped somewhere inside the cover set, so I imagine it was phased out quickly in favour of Type 2. What is interesting is that IBM chose a different approach to Datamaster for its electronics. It has a 24x4 key matrix, and the controller is split into a capacitance-sensing driver and demultiplexer on the pad card, and a separate daughterboard with an Intel 8048 as its controller. The reason for this design may be explained by the IBM 5291/5292's existence.A telltale sign from the outside is that its original cable's 180° 5-pin DIN plug has no black plastic jacket like Type 2. The keyboard also has a reset line, which the IBM PC Technical Reference implies was not used[24] and is entirely dropped by Type 2.Another IBM Personal Computer[ASK]Type 2 F/XT (bottom)[ASK]Type 2 F/XT CSA (top)[ASK]Type 2 F/XT CSA (bottom)[ASK]Type 2 F/XT pad card[25]The Type 2 design is what most F/XTs actually are, and certainly by the time of PC/XT, the only one available. As already mentioned, their DIN plugs have a plastic jacket and lack a reset line. But much has changed internally too, perhaps anarchonistic in some ways. It reverts to using a 12x8 matrix like Datamaster's, though configured differently. The controller is unified with the pad card once again, though of course still implementing the IBM PC Mode 1 interface.5291 Model 1 (illustration of)[26]The IBM 5291 Model 1 Display Station and 5292 Color Display Station were both 5250-family terminals announced on 6th September 1982. They are plug-compatible with the '70s IBM 5251 Display Station (model 11), [29][30] though the 5291 was intended as a low-cost replacement and the 5292 as a colour-enhanced supplement. 5291 Model 2 joined them on 2nd October 1984,[31] which was functionally identical to 5291-1 but smaller, more ergonomic, and with a relocatable screen, whereas 5291's was tightly integrated into the base unit.529X CSA (bottom)[32]529X capsense driver[32]529X feet (all extended)[ASK]529X feet (various levels)[ASK]The 529X keyboard is a fun one. It's like the F/XT but dialled up to eleven. It has considerable bezels just like the 5324's, though with a slightly smaller 'forehead'. But it also has absurd three-setting riser feet, the longest of an IBM keyboard I have seen. Perhaps both of these facts lend themselves to the 529X keyboard's common nickname - the "bigfoot" Model F. The key nomenclature is back to being 5250-style, given 5291's and 5292's application. The 529X keyboard CSA is the same as the Type 1 F/XT's but without the controller daughtercard. Instead, the terminal itself would be its controller, making the 529X keyboard effectively "brainless" on their own. This is where I can see why IBM designed the Type 1 F/XT differently from Datamaster - more component commonality between higher-volume products. Both PC and (in my observations) at least 5291 were more so than Datamaster. Ultimately, the simpler, more elegant Type 2 solution won out for PCs, though.The 5291-2 and 5292 shared the same completely detachable keyboard with a DA-15 plug, dubbed the Type 2 529X keyboard. 5291-1's Type 1 was instead always tethered, as its cable connected to a 14-pin IDC-style header inside the terminal, meaning the terminal has to be opened to detach it. The Type 2 is typically the far more common of the two today.Lexmark-produced rear label[33]Lexmark-refurbed rear label[32]Of all the keyboards discussed today, the 529X keyboard was produced the longest. Lexmark, which was founded from IBM Information Products Corporation's divestiture on 27th March 1991,[34] produced 529X keyboards into at least mid-1994. This also makes it one of the last Model Fs in production in general. Lexmark also refurbished existing 529X keyboards into 1996, their final year in the keyboard business. Lexmark-produced and Lexmark-refurbished 529X keyboards can usually be distinguished by the latter being mislabelled "Model M" on their rear labels instead of "F".IBM 9001 (formerly CS/9000)[35]The IBM Instruments Computer System 9000 (CS/9000, also known simply as the System 9000) was a Motorola 68000-powered laboratory computer introduced in May 1982. It was notable for its vertical stack including an integrated printer/plotter and a 57-key membrane touch panel. On 21st February 1984, IBM introduced the System 9002 Desk-Top Computer and renamed the CS/9000 to the System 9001 Bench-Top Computer. In Q2 1985, the System 9003 Industrial-Floor Computer also joined them.[36]The 9002 was designed to be a space-saving alternative to the now-9001, shedding the printer/plotter and integrating the membrane touch panel into the keyboard itself.[37] The 9003 was intended for use in manufacturing and process control applications, being able to operate as standalone or link with an IBM host processor via Systems Network Architecture (SNA). The entire 9000 family was withdrawn effective 2nd December 1986,[38] as ultimately all three members were unsuccessful in their respective markets.9001 Standard Keyboard (top)[39]9001 Standard Keyboard (bottom)[40]The CS/9000 and 9001 used the IBM System 9000 Standard Keyboard, which was designed to sit on top of a protrusion from the host computer. The Standard Keyboard notably sports a rectangular "IBM System 9000" branding, no flip-out riser feet, a cable that sprouts from the left, and a choke just before the cable's DIN plug. Otherwise, it is the same and electrically compatible with the standard F/XT.9002 Hybrid Keyboard[35]The 9002's keyboard - the IBM System 9002 Hybrid Keyboard - is a lot more interesting, though. As aforementioned, this keyboard notably integrates the 57-key membrane touch panel into the keyboard itself. Presumably, "Hybrid" refers to its nature of having both a buckling-spring keyboard and the touch panel. The resultant design is very reminiscent of the IBM 104-key Model F Converged Keyboard used for the IBM 3290 Information Panel and 5085 Graphics Processor, with the panel taking the place of the 24-function-key bank but retaining its noticable bezels and two-stage riser feet. Despite this, the keyboard itself remains the F/XT-style assembly.Whilst a 9002 computer has turned up in recent times, the keyboard has not, nor are there any photos of the keyboard from outside the 1980s. No one that I know owns one to test it or dig inside, thus its electronics remain a mystery to me. In my 'professional' opinion, the 9002 Hybrid Keyboard is the rarest Model F keyboard known, perhaps at most tied with another keyboard I plan to talk about soon. At least all the other known variants have been contemporaneously pictured...At present, the 9003 or its keyboard also remain unseen to me. Computerworld's reporting suggests the keyboard and 57-key touch panel were separate, just like the 9001.[41]Portable Personal ComputerThe IBM Portable Personal Computer[42]On 16th February 1984, IBM announced the 5155 Portable Personal Computer. It is essentially a PC/XT assembled into a luggable form and given a cute 9" amber CRT display and one or two now-half-height 5¼" floppy diskette drives.[43] It was IBM's answer to the Compaq Portable, one of the first IBM PC clones that launched just under a year earlier and happened to be in the same form factor.Portable PC Keyboard (top)[ASK]Portable PC Keyboard CSA (bottom)[ASK]Compared to the original F/XT, the 5155's version is housed in an all-plastic, two-tone cover set with a compartment to stuff its cable into, its base plate is a shiny, silvery aluminium instead of chromated steel, and it has a 6-pin modular plug instead of DIN. This results in the keyboard being considerably lighter and sounding somewhat higher-pitched than the original. The cover set can also be opened toolessly as the dark plastic bezel surrounding the keys can be lifted at any time. Electrically, the keyboard remains unchanged, and it can be passively adapted to 5-pin DIN if so desired.When not in use, the keyboard should be mounted upright to the front of the 5155, covering its entire front. The keyboard has two clips towards the top that are used to release it and allow it to pivot down. You can additionally deploy its riser feet to completely detach the keyboard from the host PC.TPC and EMRThe IBM Tempest PC (TPC) family are IBM PC-related products that were designed or modified to qualify under the TEMPEST program. TEMPEST is a NATO-recognised, United States National Security Agency specification regarding protecting against spying with electronic equipment. In particular, qualifying systems are designed not to radiate electromagnetic emanations to counter Van Eck phreaking. IBM referred to such systems as being 'TEMPESTed', usually adding special covers and filters to meet the requirements. The TPC family ultimately included the IBM 4450 TPC1 (TEMPESTed PC), 4455 TPC2 (PC/XT), 4456 TPC3 (3270 PC), 4459 TPC4 (PC/AT), and 4460 TPC5 (3270 PC/AT).[44]TPC1 and TPC2 indeed come with an F/XT variant named TPC Keyboard I and TPC Keyboard II, respectively, which despite their name and part numbers, do not differ from each other. Additionally, an IBM EMR Keyboard and EMR Keyboard II are known, although it is presently unclear to me what exactly those two were used for (ie., are they also TPC family products or are they intended for TEMPESTed IBM systems outside of the TPC family).TPC1 CSA (bottom)[49]TPC2 CSA (bottom)[46]All four keyboards have clay covering the controller, hardier, non-coiled cables, and unique plugs compared to their 'civilian' counterparts. EMR I uniquely used a 180° 5-pin DIN plug not unlike the Type 1 F/XT's, whereas the other three (and TPCs 3 through 5) used a DE-9 connector instead. This means EMR I is not physically compatible with the known TPCs. EMR II, however, seems to be identical to TPC1 and TPC2.Regarding the PCs themselves, at least based on Cathode Ray Dude's analysis on the TPC4 and comparison with a standard PC/AT, they appear to be mostly as you would expect from the standard models inside. The motherboard, power supply and ISA card complement were typical, and the differences lay with the reinforced outer casing, the power switch location and function, and some buffer space between the rear I/O and the actual back of the TPC.[51]5531 keyboard (top)[52]5531 keyboard Oak FTM keyswitches[53]5531 keyboard rear label[54]It is worth briefly mentioning the IBM 5531 Industrial Computer and its keyboard. The IBM 5531 Industrial Computer was an industrialised version of the PC/XT, introduced on 1st May 1984. It was intended for use on factory floors and accordingly designed to be more resistant to harsher physical conditions.[55] Being PC/XT-based, it thus received an XT-style keyboard. Whilst it superficially looks like an industrial-grey version of the F/XT, the keyboard is of an unrelated design and not considered a Model F keyboard. It was made by Oak Switch Systems for IBM, using their Full-Travel Membrane (FTM) keyswitches. To easily tell it a part from the F/XT, note its flatter appearance and the lack of curvature on the separator between the F-keys and the rest of the keys. This is not to say this keyboard does not have any merit; just note that it is indeed not a Model F and you should not expect it to be like one.Big thanks to RetroAND (bitspassats.com) for our mutual conversations over the last year or so on Datamaster, and their assistance with ensuring the facts surrounding Datamaster inside this article and elsewhere are as best as they could be.InternalASK Keyboard TimelineIBM Model F keyboards Major IBM typewriter & keyboard modelsExternalDavid J. blocks.html_en: 45 years ago today, on 12th August 1981, the computing landscape changed forever. IBM launched the Personal Computer (type 5150), which kickstarted a series of events that defined what most people today think a PC is, even if it was not the first computer to be called "personal". It was the vessel that kickstarted x86's popularity in computing at offices and homes alike. The PC's long-term staying power was not a feat IBM achieved alone - the IBM-compatible "clone" PC market is what helped sustain the ecosystem's prominence. Personally, I like to think a big part of the PC's initial success was its keyboard. Not the perfect layout as most may agree, but certainly a competent, well-built keyboard - the Model F/XT. Thus to celebrate, in the most appropriate way for Admiral Shark's Keyboards, we will look at this keyboard, where it came from, and what it became. Of course, with context as needed, including what led to the IBM PC, and both who and what was behind it.

blocks.html_en: Before the PC, IBM released products adjacent to a personal computer, and toyed with the idea of a personal computer throughout the 1970s. The PC's type number, 5150, places it in the lineage of the 5100 Portable Computer, and the 5110 and 5120 Computing Systems. 5100 in turn is an evolution of a prototype computer known as SCAMP (Special Computer APL Machine Portable), which was developed at the IBM Palo Alto Scientific Center in 1973.[4] William C. Lowe, an executive in the IBM General Systems Division (GSD) at the time, was considered instrumental in foresting this prototype. The 5100 was touted as a "personal computer" by some in the media, but it was a very expensive and not accessible to many people. It was notable for being portable though (for 1975), emphasised as IBM's smallest computing system to date.[5]

blocks.html_en: The Datamaster keyboard establishes the basis for every other keyboard discussed today. It is presently the earliest confirmed Model F keyboard implementation to make it to market, which would soon expand into an entire family of IBM flagship keyboards prominent for the first half of the '80s. They all use capacitive buckling springs, a keyswitch design by Richard Hunter Haris (U.S. utility patent 4,118,611), where pressing a key compresses a metal coil spring underneath in a way that it eventually "catastrophically" buckles, which in turn pivots a small plate made of a capacitive material atop a capacitance-sensing PCB called a "pad card". The keyboard assembly this all sits in is largely metallic, with a steel frame holding the keyswitch barrels at the top, and a usually-chromated steel base plate at the bottom.

blocks.html_en: The 5322 keyboard is a complete sub-assembly (CSA) that sits inside the host Datamaster. The keys are arranged in a layout derived from the Model B-based IBM 5251/5252 Display Station Typewriter Keyboard, which was IBM's most immediate and common pre-Datamaster major keyboard design. The aforementioned pad card bears a 12x8 key matrix and an Intel 8048 as its controller. The keyboard uses a parallel-style interface where an inverted 7-bit scancode is sent across separate scanbit lines together. Like its layout, its scancodes are also derived from the 5250 family. On the receiving end, according to RetroAND (bitspassats.com), the Datamaster has an 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface configured for mode 1 input. As the keyboard is completely internalised, it connects directly to the 5322 motherboard (CPU planar board) via an 8x2 header.

blocks.html_en: As the 5324 is a distributed system, its version of the keyboard is discrete, connecting to its host via a DB-25-terminating cable. Chronologically, this was released after the PC, so it derives its styling from the PC's keyboard, but with a considerably enlarged cover set and slightly longer riser feet. It may sometimes be confused with the IBM 5291/5292 keyboard also discussed later, but the 5324 keyboard has the larger bezel between them, to the point it sometimes gets nicknamed the "bezelmaster" Model F keyboard. The 5324 keyboard reuses the 5322's keyboard CSAs. But the 5324 keyboard adds a "keyboard adapter card" before its external cable. As explained to me by RetroAND, it has positive buffers and double negations for the control signals, likely to reduce noise. In effect, it prepares a design that was originally integrated into something, to be a distributed design that requires a longer cable.

blocks.html_en: Roll back the clock to July 1980: Lowe pitched the idea of a small, low-cost business and consumer computer to IBM CEO Frank Cary, who subsequently gave him a month to develop a prototype and to launch the finished product in a year. It was dubbed "Project Chess". Lowe was promoted soon after, so Chess fell to Philip Donald (Don) Estridge. Both have been referred to as the "Father of the IBM PC".[17][18] The team consisted of about twelve engineers, who were famously able to develop the PC outside of IBM's typical processes, ultimately allowing them to meet the one-year deadline, rather than complete it in 2 to 5 years like most other IBM systems of the time.

blocks.html_en: As you know, the IBM 5150 Personal Computer was released 45 years ago today. Its importance cannot be overstated. Its open architecture and use of the 8086-sibling Intel 8088 established one of the most popular and long-lived computer ecosystems. For better or worse nowadays, the combination of it and a Microsoft-sourced operating system is still relevant thanks to this. To me personally, learning about it and tinkering with its descendants are the backdrop to my technical interests and knowledge. The PC was joined by the IBM 5160 Personal Computer XT (PC/XT) on 8th March 1983. Over the original PC, the PC/XT adds a built-in hard drive and 3 expansion slots,[20] otherwise being a very similar design. Whilst there are many factors as to why the PC succeeded, it was certainly aided by the inclusion of a competent keyboard.

blocks.html_en: The IBM Personal Computer Keyboard is often colloquially referred to as the "XT keyboard" or "Model F/XT", using its association with the PC/XT to differentiate it from the later IBM Personal Computer AT Keyboard ("Model F/AT"). Components of the F/XT can also be referred to as being "XT". At its core, the F/XT has a keyboard assembly much like the Datamaster's, but it adopted a new serial-based protocol retroactively called IBM PC Mode 1 (also known as the "XT keyboard interface", naturally). blocks.html_en: The 529X keyboard is a fun one. It's like the F/XT but dialled up to eleven. It has considerable bezels just like the 5324's, though with a slightly smaller 'forehead'. But it also has absurd three-setting riser feet, the longest of an IBM keyboard I have seen. Perhaps both of these facts lend themselves to the 529X keyboard's common nickname - the "bigfoot" Model F. The key nomenclature is back to being 5250-style, given 5291's and 5292's application. The 529X keyboard CSA is the same as the Type 1 F/XT's but without the controller daughtercard. Instead, the terminal itself would be its controller, making the 529X keyboard effectively "brainless" on their own. This is where I can see why IBM designed the Type 1 F/XT differently from Datamaster - more component commonality between higher-volume products. Both PC and (in my observations) at least 5291 were more so than Datamaster. Ultimately, the simpler, more elegant Type 2 solution won out for PCs, though.

As aforementioned, this keyboard notably integrates the 57-key membrane touch panel into the keyboard itself. blocks.html_en: Compared to the original F/XT, the 5155's version is housed in an all-plastic, two-tone cover set with a compartment to stuff its cable into, its base plate is a shiny, silvery aluminium instead of chromated steel, and it has a 6-pin modular plug instead of DIN. blocks.html_en: The IBM Tempest PC (TPC) family are IBM PC-related products that were designed or modified to qualify under the TEMPEST program. TEMPEST is a NATO-recognised, United States National Security Agency specification regarding protecting against spying with electronic equipment. In particular, qualifying systems are designed not to radiate electromagnetic emanations to counter Van Eck phreaking. IBM referred to such systems as being 'TEMPESTed', usually adding special covers and filters to meet the requirements. The TPC family ultimately included the IBM 4450 TPC1 (TEMPESTed PC), 4455 TPC2 (PC/XT), 4456 TPC3 (3270 PC), 4459 TPC4 (PC/AT), and 4460 TPC5 (3270 PC/AT).[44]

blocks.html_en: It is worth briefly mentioning the IBM 5531 Industrial Computer and its keyboard. The IBM 5531 Industrial Computer was an industrialised version of the PC/XT, introduced on 1st May 1984. It was intended for use on factory floors and accordingly designed to be more resistant to harsher physical conditions.[55] Being PC/XT-based, it thus received an XT-style keyboard. Whilst it superficially looks like an industrial-grey version of the F/XT, the keyboard is of an unrelated design and not considered a Model F keyboard. It was made by Oak Switch Systems for IBM, using their Full-Travel Membrane (FTM) keyswitches. To easily tell it a part from the F/XT, note its flatter appearance and the lack of curvature on the separator between the F-keys and the rest of the keys. This is not to say this keyboard does not have any merit; just note that it is indeed not a Model F and you should not expect it to be like one.

content_html_zh:
• 发布于 2026 年 8 月 12 日
  • 更新于 2026 年 8 月 13 日
  • 预计。阅读时间：约20-24分钟

45 年前的今天，即 1981 年 8 月 12 日，计算格局发生了永远的变化。 IBM 推出了个人计算机（5150 型），引发了一系列事件，定义了当今大多数人对 PC 的看法，即使它不是第一台被称为“个人”的计算机。 正是它启动了 x86 在办公室和家庭计算领域的普及。 PC 的长期持久力并不是 IBM 独自实现的壮举 - IBM 兼容的“克隆”PC 市场有助于维持该生态系统的突出地位。 就我个人而言，我认为 PC 最初的成功很大一部分归功于它的键盘。 虽然不是大多数人都同意的完美布局，但绝对是一款功能强大、制作精良的键盘 - Model F/XT。 因此，为了以最适合 Admiral Shark's Keyboards 的方式庆祝，我们将看看这款键盘，它来自哪里，以及它变成了什么。 当然，根据需要提供上下文，包括 IBM PC 的诞生及其背后的人物和事物。

内容

在 PC 诞生之前，IBM 就发布了与个人电脑类似的产品，并在整个 20 世纪 70 年代一直在尝试个人电脑的想法。 PC 的型号为 5150，它属于 5100 便携式计算机以及 5110 和 5120 计算系统的系列。 5100 又是 SCAMP（便携式 APL 专用计算机）原型计算机的演变，该计算机于 1973 年在 IBM 帕洛阿尔托科学中心开发。 [4]威廉·C. Lowe 是当时 IBM 通用系统部门 (GSD) 的一名高管，他被认为在这个原型的开发过程中发挥了重要作用。 5100 被一些媒体吹捧为“个人电脑”，但它非常昂贵，很多人都买不起。 它以便携性而闻名（1975 年），被强调为 IBM 迄今为止最小的计算系统。 [5]

汤米·R。 Hardy 现已成为 IBM 资深设计师，他对个人电脑提出了一些临时想法，包括 1976 年的“Yellow Bird”和 1977 年的“Aquarius”，这两款电脑的外形都隐约呈楔形，与后来的 Commodore VIC-20、64 等类似，尽管更大。 Aquarius 甚至制作了预生产原型，但最终因对其使用气泡内存模块缺乏信心而被驳回。 当 Atari 的 8 位计算机于 1979 年推出时，IBM 也考虑收购 Atari 并利用 800 作为 PC 的基础。 Hardy 为此构思了一款珍珠白色的 IBM 品牌 800，[6] 但这个想法没有进一步发展。 不过，下一件大事是 Datamaster。

讨论 PC 及其键盘就不可能不谈论 IBM System/23 Datamaster，这是对 IBM 具有影响力的经验，帮助他们开发 PC 及其键盘。 5322 是最初的“桌面”（一体式）Datamaster，于 1981 年 7 月发布。 随后于 1982 年 5 月 18 日发布了 5324“floortop”（塔式）Datamaster。 [10]它们是基于 Intel 8085 的微型计算机，旨在运行用 BASIC 编写的业务应用程序。

Datamaster 的开发始于 1978 年 2 月，其硬件于 1980 年 7 月准备就绪。 然而，正如 IBM 工程师 David J. 回忆的那样。 Bradley 曾参与 Datamaster 的开发工作，由于 IBM 决定开发 Datamaster 的 BASIC，使其更符合 IBM System/34 中端计算机的实现，因此 Datamaster 的发布比 PC 推迟了一年，仅推迟了一个月。 [11] 5322 的造型归功于 Hardy，其美国设计专利 (275,285) 于 1980 年 2 月 4 日申请。 该阶段的设计很大程度上类似于成品，尽管键盘布局略有不同，有额外的按键和非步进式 Enter 键。 如果 5324 的设计专利存在的话，我在研究过程中找不到它们。

Datamaster 键盘为今天讨论的所有其他键盘奠定了基础。 它是目前最早确认投放市场的 Model F 键盘，很快就会扩展到整个 80 年代上半叶流行的 IBM 旗舰键盘系列。 它们都使用电容式屈曲弹簧，这是 Richard Hunter Haris 设计的按键开关（美国实用专利 4,118,611），按下按键会压缩下方的金属螺旋弹簧，最终“灾难性”地屈曲，从而使位于电容感应 PCB（称为“垫卡”）顶部的电容材料制成的小板旋转。 这一切所采用的键盘组件主要是金属的，钢框架将按键开关筒固定在顶部，底部通常是铬酸盐钢底板。

5322 键盘是位于主机 Datamaster 内部的完整子组件 (CSA)。 按键的布局源自基于 B 型的 IBM 5251/5252 显示站打字机键盘，这是 IBM 最直接、最常见的前 Datamaster 主要键盘设计。 上述的pad卡带有一个12x8的按键矩阵和一个Intel 8048作为其控制器。 键盘使用并行式接口，其中反转的 7 位扫描码通过单独的扫描位线一起发送。 与其布局一样，其扫描码也源自 5250 系列。 根据 RetroAND (bitspassats.com) 的说法，在接收端，Datamaster 有一个配置为模式 1 输入的 8255 可编程外设接口。 由于键盘已完全内置，因此它通过 8x2 接头直接连接到 5322 主板（CPU 主板）。

由于 5324 是分布式系统，因此其键盘版本是离散的，通过 DB-25 端接电缆连接到其主机。 按时间顺序，它是在 PC 之后发布的，因此它的造型源自 PC 的键盘，但具有相当大的外壳组和稍长的立脚。 它有时可能会与稍后讨论的 IBM 5291/5292 键盘相混淆，但 5324 键盘在它们之间具有更大的边框，以至于它有时被昵称为“bezelmaster”F 型键盘。 5324 键盘重复使用了 5322 的键盘 CSA。 但5324键盘在其外接电缆之前增加了一个“键盘适配卡”。 正如 RetroAND 向我解释的那样，它对控制信号有正缓冲器和双重否定，可能会减少噪音。 实际上，它准备了一个最初集成到某些东西中的设计，成为需要更长电缆的分布式设计。

个人电脑

时间回到 1980 年 7 月：Lowe 向 IBM 首席执行官 Frank Cary 提出了小型、低成本的商用和消费计算机的想法，后者随后给了他一个月的时间来开发原型，并在一年内推出成品。 它被称为“国际象棋计划”。 洛很快就升职了，所以国际象棋就落到了菲利普·唐纳德·埃斯特里奇的手中。 两人都被称为“IBM PC 之父”。[17][18]该团队由大约 12 名工程师组成，他们以能够在 IBM 典型流程之外开发 PC 而闻名，最终使他们能够在一年的期限内完成，而不是像当时大多数其他 IBM 系统那样在 2 到 5 年内完成。

PC 的最早草图于 1980 年 8 月 10 日发布，直到最近才发布。 他们表明，PC 的许多内容在早期就已确定，包括使用 Intel 8088、五个扩展插槽、两个软盘驱动器、使用 ASCII 代替 EBCDIC，以及基于 F 型的独立键盘。 当然，存在一些显着的差异，包括显示控制器、电源装置在 PC 内的位置，以及最初指定为 8 英寸软盘驱动器而不是 5 ¼ 英寸。[19]

为了实现他们的目标，团队还得到了开发 Datamaster 和使用现成组件的先前经验的帮助。 PC 对 Intel CPU、各种 Intel 支持控制器和定时器以及 8 位 ISA 总线的使用源自 Datamaster 对类似技术的使用。 选择具有 20 位/1MB 地址空间的 8088 主要是因为 Datamaster 的 8085 及其 16 位/64KB 地址空间的问题。 选择 8088 而不是 8086 是因为只需支持 8 位数据总线而不是 16 位数据总线即可节省成本。[11]

如您所知，IBM 5150 个人计算机于 45 年前的今天发布。 它的重要性怎么强调都不为过。 其开放式架构和对 8086 兄弟英特尔 8088 的使用建立了最流行和最长寿的计算机生态系统之一。 如今，无论好坏，它与微软来源的操作系统的结合仍然具有重要意义。 对我个人而言，了解它并修改它的后代是我技术兴趣和知识的背景。 1983 年 3 月 8 日，IBM 5160 个人计算机 XT (PC/XT) 加入了 PC 的行列。 在原来的 PC 上，PC/XT 增加了一个内置硬盘驱动器和 3 个扩展插槽，[20] 其他方面的设计非常相似。 虽然 PC 的成功有很多因素，但它肯定得益于功能强大的键盘。

IBM 个人计算机键盘通常通俗地称为“XT 键盘”或“F/XT 型”，利用其与 PC/XT 的关联来区别于后来的 IBM 个人计算机 AT 键盘（“F/AT 型”）。 F/XT 的组件也可称为“XT”。 F/XT 的核心键盘组件与 Datamaster 非常相似，但它采用了一种新的基于串行的协议，追溯称为 IBM PC Mode 1（自然也称为“XT 键盘接口”）。 它发出 9 位数据包，促进 IBM 扫描码集 1。 键帽命名法已更改为 ASCII 样式，而不是 EBCDIC。 在前面提到的草图中，界面和命名法从一开始就决定了，但也有人认为它们可以通过消除最左边的功能键库来节省设计成本，[19]但这并没有实现。

我无法找到 PC 本身的任何设计专利（如果存在的话），但键盘的（美国设计专利 278,063）是已知的。 汤米·哈迪 (Tommy Hardy) 以及爱德华·张伯伦 (Edward Chamberlain)、尼古拉斯·M·肯尼迪 (Nicholas M. 莱昂，彼得·J. Mendel（后来从事许多其他与键盘相关的 IBM 产品设计）和 Michael H. 锋利的。 已知原始 F/XT 的两个主要变体，两者都有自己的细微差别以及与 Datamaster 键盘的差异或相似之处。 它们被称为类型 1 和类型 2。

最初的设计，Type 1，如今非常罕见。 我只见过其芯片上或封面内某处印有“81”日期代码的示例，所以我想它很快就会被淘汰，取而代之的是 Type 2。 有趣的是，IBM 为其电子产品选择了不同的 Datamaster 方法。 它有一个 24x4 按键矩阵，控制器分为电容感应驱动器和垫卡上的解复用器，以及一个以 Intel 8048 作为控制器的独立子板。 IBM 5291/5292 的存在可以解释这种设计的原因。

从外观上可以看出，其原始电缆的 180° 5 针 DIN 插头没有像 2 型那样的黑色塑料护套。 键盘还有一条重置线，IBM PC 技术参考暗示未使用该线[24]，并且完全被 Type 2 丢弃。

Type 2 设计是大多数 F/XT 的实际设计，当然到了 PC/XT 时代，这是唯一可用的设计。 正如已经提到的，它们的 DIN 插头有塑料护套，并且没有复位线。 但内部也发生了很大变化，在某些方面或许是无政府主义的。 它恢复为使用像 Datamaster 那样的 12x8 矩阵，尽管配置不同。 控制器再次与 pad 卡统一，当然仍然实现 IBM PC Mode 1 接口。

IBM 5291 Model 1 Display Station 和 5292 Color Display Station 都是 1982 年 9 月 6 日发布的 5250 系列终端。 它们与 70 年代 IBM 5251 显示站（型号 11）[29][30] 兼容，尽管 5291 旨在作为低成本替代品，而 5292 则作为色彩增强补充。 5291 Model 2 于 1984 年 10 月 2 日加入其中，[31] 其功能与 5291-1 相同，但更小、更符合人体工程学，并且具有可重新定位的屏幕，而 5291 则紧密集成到基本单元中。

529X 键盘是一款有趣的键盘。 它类似于 F/XT，但拨至 11。 它具有与 5324 类似的相当大的边框，但“额头”稍小一些。 但它也有荒谬的三设置立脚，这是我见过的最长的 IBM 键盘。 也许这两个事实都为 529X 键盘带来了一个常见的绰号——“大脚”Model F。 鉴于 5291 和 5292 的应用，关键命名法又回到了 5250 风格。 529X 键盘 CSA 与 Type 1 F/XT 相同，但没有控制器子卡。 相反，终端本身就是它的控制器，这使得 529X 键盘本身实际上是“无脑”的。 这就是我可以理解为什么 IBM 设计的 Type 1 F/XT 与 Datamaster 不同的原因——大批量产品之间有更多的组件通用性。 PC 和（根据我的观察）至少 5291 都比 Datamaster 更重要。 不过，最终，更简单、更优雅的 Type 2 解决方案在 PC 上胜出。

5291-2 和 5292 共享相同的带有 DA-15 插头的完全可拆卸键盘，称为 Type 2 529X 键盘。 相反，5291-1 的 Type 1 始终受到束缚，因为它的电缆连接到终端内的 14 针 IDC 式接头，这意味着必须打开终端才能将其拆下。 2 型通常是当今这两种类型中更为常见的一种。

在今天讨论的所有键盘中，529X键盘的生产时间最长。 Lexmark 于 1991 年 3 月 27 日从 IBM Information Products Corporation 剥离后成立，[34] 至少在 1994 年中期生产 529X 键盘。 这也使其成为最后生产的 Model F 之一。 Lexmark 还在 1996 年翻新了现有的 529X 键盘，这是他们在键盘业务上的最后一年。 Lexmark 生产的 529X 键盘和 Lexmark 翻新的 529X 键盘通常可以通过后标签上错误地标记为“Model M”而不是“F”来区分。

IBM Instruments Computer System 9000（CS/9000，也简称为 System 9000）是一款由 Motorola 68000 驱动的实验室计算机，于 1982 年 5 月推出。 它以其垂直堆栈而闻名，其中包括集成打印机/绘图仪和 57 键薄膜触摸面板。 1984 年 2 月 21 日，IBM 推出 System 9002 台式计算机，并将 CS/9000 更名为 System 9001 台式计算机。 1985 年第二季度，System 9003 工业地面计算机也加入其中。[36]

9002 被设计为现在 9001 的节省空间替代品，去掉了打印机/绘图仪并将薄膜触摸面板集成到键盘本身中。 [37] 9003 旨在用于制造和过程控制应用，能够独立运行或通过系统网络架构 (SNA) 与 IBM 主机处理器连接。 整个 9000 系列于 1986 年 12 月 2 日退出，[38] 因为最终所有三个成员在各自的市场上都没有取得成功。

CS/9000 和 9001 使用 IBM System 9000 标准键盘，该键盘设计为位于主机突出部的顶部。 标准键盘特别带有矩形“IBM System 9000”品牌标识，没有翻转式立管脚，电缆从左侧伸出，电缆 DIN 插头前有一个扼流圈。 其他方面与标准 F/XT 相同且电气兼容。

不过，9002 的键盘——IBM System 9002 混合键盘——要有趣得多。 如上所述，这款键盘特别将 57 键薄膜触摸屏集成到键盘本身中。 据推测，“混合”指的是其同时具有屈曲弹簧键盘和触摸面板的性质。 由此产生的设计非常让人想起用于 IBM 3290 信息面板和 5085 图形处理器的 IBM 104 键 F 型融合键盘，该面板取代了 24 个功能键组，但保留了其引人注目的边框和两级提升脚。 尽管如此，键盘本身仍然是 F/XT 风格的组件。

虽然最近出现了 9002 计算机，但键盘却没有出现，也没有任何 20 世纪 80 年代以外的键盘照片。 据我所知，没有人拥有一个来测试它或挖掘它的内部，因此它的电子设备对我来说仍然是一个谜。 在我的“专业”观点中，9002 混合键盘是已知最稀有的 F 型键盘，也许最多与我计划很快讨论的另一款键盘并列。 至少所有其他已知的变体都已同时被拍摄出来......

目前，我还没有看到9003或其键盘。 Computerworld 的报道表明键盘和 57 键触摸面板是分开的，就像 9001 一样。[41]

便携式个人电脑

1984 年 2 月 16 日，IBM 发布了 5155 便携式个人计算机。 它本质上是一台组装成可携带形式的 PC/XT，并配有可爱的 9 英寸琥珀色 CRT 显示器和一个或两个现在半高的 5 ¼ 英寸软盘驱动器。 [43]这是 IBM 对 Compaq Portable 的回应，Compaq Portable 是最早的 IBM PC 克隆产品之一，于不到一年前推出，并且外形尺寸相同。

与原来的 F/XT 相比，5155 的版本采用全塑料双色调盖套件，并带有一个可将电缆塞入的隔间，其底板是闪亮的银色铝而不是铬酸盐钢，并且具有 6 针模块化插头而不是 DIN。 这使得键盘比原来的键盘要轻得多，而且听起来音调更高。 由于按键周围的深色塑料边框可以随时提起，因此无需任何工具即可打开盖子组。 在电气方面，键盘保持不变，如果需要，可以被动适应 5 针 DIN。

不使用时，键盘应直立安装到 5155 的正面，覆盖其整个正面。 键盘顶部有两个夹子，用于释放键盘并使其向下旋转。 您还可以部署其提升脚，将键盘与主机完全分离。

TPC 和 EMR

IBM Tempest PC (TPC) 系列是 IBM PC 相关产品，经过设计或修改，符合 TEMPEST 计划的资格。 TEMPEST 是北约认可的美国国家安全局规范，涉及防止电子设备间谍活动。 特别是，资格系统的设计不会辐射电磁辐射，以对抗范埃克窃听行为。 IBM 将此类系统称为“TEMPESTed”，通常会添加特殊的盖子和过滤器来满足要求。 TPC 系列最终包括 IBM 4450 TPC1 (TEMPESTed PC)、4455 TPC2 (PC/XT)、4456 TPC3 (3270 PC)、4459 TPC4 (PC/AT) 和 4460 TPC5 (3270 PC/AT)。 [44]

TPC1 和 TPC2 确实配备了分别名为 TPC 键盘 I 和 TPC 键盘 II 的 F/XT 变体，尽管它们的名称和部件号不同，但它们彼此没有区别。 此外，IBM EMR 键盘和 EMR 键盘 II 是已知的，尽管目前我还不清楚这两个键盘的具体用途（即它们是否也是 TPC 系列产品，或者它们是否用于 TPC 系列之外的 TEMPESTed IBM 系统）。

与“民用”键盘相比，所有四个键盘的控制器都覆盖有粘土，更坚固，非盘绕电缆，以及独特的插头。 EMR I 独特地使用了 180° 5 针 DIN 插头，与 Type 1 F/XT 不同，而其他三个（以及 TPC 3 至 5）则使用 DE-9 连接器。 这意味着 EMR I 与已知的 TPC 物理上不兼容。 然而，EMR II 似乎与 TPC1 和 TPC2 相同。

关于 PC 本身，至少根据 Cathode Ray Dude 对 TPC4 的分析以及与标准 PC/AT 的比较，它们似乎与您对内部标准型号的预期基本一致。 主板、电源和ISA卡配件都是典型的，区别在于加固的外壳、电源开关的位置和功能，以及后部I/O和TPC实际背面之间的一些缓冲空间。 [51]

值得简单提及的是 IBM 5531 工业计算机及其键盘。 IBM 5531 工业计算机是 PC/XT 的工业化版本，于 1984 年 5 月 1 日推出。 它旨在用于工厂车间，因此设计得更能抵抗更恶劣的物理条件。 [55]由于它基于 PC/XT，因此配备了 XT 风格的键盘。 虽然它表面上看起来像 F/XT 的工业灰色版本，但键盘的设计不相关，不被视为 F 型键盘。 它是由 Oak Switch Systems 为 IBM 使用其全行程薄膜 (FTM) 按键开关制造的。 为了轻松区分它与 F/XT 的区别，请注意其更平坦的外观以及 F 键和其余键之间的分隔线上没有弯曲。 这并不是说这个键盘没有任何优点；请注意，它确实不是 Model F，您不应期望它与 Model F 类似。
